summary: An exhaustive clinical guide to lens-related, open-angle, and closed-angle secondary glaucomas. This poster details the mechanisms, clinical presentations, and multi-modal treatment strategies for these complex ocular conditions.

rows: The enlarging lens causes pupillary block and anterior bowing of the iris, with 2° angle closure. In an eye of normal axial length, this occurs 2° to an intumescent cataractous lens; in a short eye, this may result simply from the normal increase in lens size with age.

iIOP, shallow AC, fixed semi-dilated pupil, swollen cataractous lens. Ipsilateral closed angle (appositional; sigma sign may be seen on indentation gonioscopy). Contralateral angle may be open with deep AC (in contrast to PACG); however, this helpful sign may not be present if the contralateral eye also has significant cataract.
Medical (topical and systemic): as for PACG. Nd-yAG PI to reverse pupillary block component. early cataract extraction is the definitive treatment—needs an experienced surgeon.

sections.title: Phacolytic Glaucoma
content: Mechanism: the hypermature cataract loses soluble lens proteins through the anterior capsule, causing trabecular obstruction and subsequent 2° open-angle glaucoma.
Clinical features: iIOP, lens protein in a deep AC (may form a pseudohypopyon), hypermature/mature cataract, open angle (with lens protein); AC tap reveals lens protein and foamy macrophages.
Treatment Medical: topical (e.g. β-blocker, α2-agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) or systemic (e.g. acetazolamide) agents, as required; consider topical steroids for associated inflammation.
Surgical: early cataract extraction—needs experienced surgeon.

sections.title: Phacoanaphylactic Uveitis
content: Mechanism: Inflammatory reaction to lens protein post-trauma or surgery (must distinguish from endophthalmitis). May cause sensitization in contralateral eye.
Clinical Features: recent trauma/surgery, exposed lens protein, AC flare + cells ± hypopyon, KPs, synechiae (PS + PAS), angle usually open (but ± PAS); IOP may be high, normal, or low.
Treatment Of inflammatory process: topical steroid (e.g. dexamethasone 0.1% hourly) and surgical removal of any retained lens fragments.
Treatment of iIOP: medical—topical (e.g. β-blocker, α2-agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) or systemic (e.g. acetazolamide) agents, as required.
For contralateral cataract: consider removal by intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCe) to reduce lens protein exposure.

sections.title: Glaucoma 2° to Lens Subluxation/Dislocation
content: Mechanism: pupillary block by anterior lens subluxation or complete dislocation into the AC; there may also be a coincident angle abnormality (e.g. Marfan’s syndrome).
Clinical features: iIOP, subluxed/dislocated lens ± corneal oedema (if acute or lenticulocorneal touch); lenticular astigmatism and variable refraction.

Treatment Positional: dilate and lie patient supine (to encourage posterior movement of lens), and constrict (to keep lens safely behind pupil); long-term miotic therapy may be needed, unless the lens dislocates safely into the vitreous.
Early lens extraction: if positional measures fail, if complete dislocation into the AC, if cataract, or if recurrent problem. Often best dealt with by a vitreoretinal approach.

sections.title: Steroid-Induced: Mechanism & Treatment
sections.content: Exogenous, and occasionally endogenous, steroids may decrease outflow facility, leading to iIOP after a few days or weeks. POAG patients are often particularly sensitive. Possible mechanisms include prostaglandin inhibition (e.g. PGF2A) and structural changes in the eCM (glycosaminoglycans) and trabecular meshwork (cross-linking of actins). History: specifically ask for steroid-containing anabolics, skin/haemorrhoid creams, inhaled steroids, or oral steroids (asthma/COPD). Treatment: Decrease frequency/potency or stop steroid (± steroid-sparing agent)—liaise with physician. If corticosteroids essential, treat as POAG. SLt may be helpful.

sections.title: Red Cell Glaucoma
content: Hyphaema (usually traumatic) leads to TM blockage.
10% risk of rebleed usually at ~5d post-injury.
Sickle-cell disease/trait patients do worse and are harder to treat (acidosis from CAIs worsens sickling).

sections.title: Red Cell Glaucoma Management
content: Of hyphaema: strict bed rest, topical steroid (e.g. dexamethasone 0.1% 6×/d), mydriatic/cycloplegic (e.g. atropine 1% 2×/d).
Of IOP: topical (e.g. β-blocker, α2-agonist, CAI) or systemic (e.g. acetazolamide) agents.
Surgical: AC paracentesis ± AC washout. In rare refractory cases, trabeculectomy.

sections.title: Ghost Cell Glaucoma
content: Mechanism: Vitreous haemorrhage leads to blockage of TM by degenerate red blood cells, usually 2–4wk after haemorrhage.
Appearance: Cells are tan-coloured (lost haemoglobin) and seen in AC and angle.
Treatment: Medical (as for POAG) is usually sufficient. If failure: AC washout + vitrectomy.

content.explanation: Traumatic Recession = 10% risk of glaucoma at 10 years. Risk increases with extent of recession.

sections.title: Angle Recession: Clinical & Screening
content: Mechanism: Blunt trauma causes angle recession and trabecular damage.
Observation: Best seen by simultaneous gonioscopy. Look for asymmetry of AC depth, pupil, and angle.
Screening: Periodic IOP check (e.g. 3mo, 6mo, yearly) if known angle recession.
Treatment: As for POAG.

sections.title: Raised Episcleral Venous Pressure
sections.content: Aqueous drainage reduced as pressure increases. Causes: Vascular abnormalities in orbit (Sturge–Weber syndrome, orbital varices), cavernous sinus (AV fistulae), or SVC obstruction. Manifestations: Unilateral/bilateral engorged episcleral veins, chemosis, proptosis, with blood in Schlemm’s canal on gonioscopy. Treatment: Directed at underlying pathology; medical/surgical IOP lowering if necessary. Surgical warning: extremely hazardous with refractory uveal effusion.

rows: Tumours
Open-angle (clogging/infiltration) or Closed-angle (rubeosis/displacement). 20% of malignant melanoma associated with iIOP.
Directed by tumour; B-scan US essential if poor posterior view. iIOP suggests poor prognosis.
Schwartz-Matsuo
Uncommon association of mild AC inflammation and iIOP (open angle) from RRD. Photoreceptor outer segments obstruct TM.
IOP/uveitis treated medically in interim; resolves rapidly with surgical repair of retinal detachment.

sections.title: Other Secondary Closed-Angle: Iridoschisis
content: Bilateral splitting/atrophy of anterior iris leaf.
Associated with nanophthalmos; usually in elderly.
Angle-closure type: treat with Nd-YAG PI.
Open-angle type: treat as POAG (due to debris blocking TM).

branches: Iris naevus (Cogan–Reese) syndrome (protrusions of iris stroma)

sections.title: ICE Syndrome Details
content: Unilateral (rarely bilateral) condition; abnormal endothelium migrates across angle, TM, and iris. Usually 20-40y old female. HSV proposed as causative.
Clinical features: Unilateral pain, blurred vision. Fine corneal guttata ('beaten metal'), corneal oedema, iris atrophy, corectopia (displaced pupil), pseudopolycoria (accessory pupil).
Gonioscopy: Broad-based PAS that may insert anterior to Schwalbe’s line.
Investigations: Consider specular microscopy for endothelial changes.
Treatment: Medical (β-blocker, α2-agonist, CAI, PGA), surgery (trabeculectomy ± augmented or tube), or cyclodestruction.

rows: Posterior Polymorphous Dystrophy (PPD)
Bilateral, dominantly inherited, detectable in childhood. Abnormal endothelium forms extensive adhesions with angle closure. 15% risk of glaucoma.
Treat glaucoma as for POAG.
Epithelial Downgrowth
Trauma/surgery allows epithelium to proliferate across corneal endothelium and angle. Similar to ICE syndrome but unchecked proliferation.
Very difficult; lower IOP as for POAG; intracameral antifibrotics (e.g. 5-FU), surgical excision. Prognosis for vision is poor.
Fuchs’ Endothelial Dystrophy
Oedema of the peripheral cornea may cause 2° angle closure.
Risk is highest in eyes with pre-existing shallow ACs.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Comprehensive Guide to Secondary Glaucomas ---
sections.content: An exhaustive clinical reference covering lens-related, open-angle, closed-angle, and iatrogenic glaucomas. This guide details mechanisms, clinical features, and multi-modal treatment strategies for secondary intraocular pressure elevations.

sections.title: Lens-Related Glaucoma Overview
sections.content: Lens-related glaucoma may result from abnormalities of lens size, lens position, release of lens protein (mature cataract/trauma/surgery), and/or the consequent inflammatory response.

branches: Normal eye: 2° to intumescent cataractous lens
Short eye: 2° to normal increase in lens size with age

sections.title: Phacomorphic: Clinical & Treatment
content: Clinical Features: iIOP, shallow AC, fixed semi-dilated pupil, swollen cataractous lens.
Ipsilateral: Closed angle (appositional; sigma sign may be seen on indentation gonioscopy).
Contralateral: Angle may be open with deep AC (contrast to PACG); sign may be absent if contralateral eye has significant cataract.
Treatment Medical: Topical and systemic (as for PACG).
Treatment Laser: Nd-yAG PI to reverse pupillary block component.
Definitive Treatment: Early cataract extraction (needs an experienced surgeon).

rows: Mechanism
Hypermature cataract loses soluble lens proteins through the anterior capsule, causing trabecular obstruction and subsequent 2° open-angle glaucoma.
Clinical Features
iIOP, lens protein in a deep AC (may form a pseudohypopyon), hypermature/mature cataract, open angle (with lens protein); AC tap reveals lens protein and foamy macrophages.
Medical Treatment
Topical (e.g. β-blocker, α2-agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) or systemic (e.g. acetazolamide) agents; consider topical steroids for associated inflammation.
Surgical Treatment
Early cataract extraction—needs experienced surgeon.

sections.title: Phacoanaphylactic Uveitis
sections.content: Mechanism: This is an inflammatory reaction to lens protein, usually following traumatic capsular rupture or post-operative retention of lens material (when it must be distinguished from endophthalmitis). This insult may also cause sensitization such that lens protein exposure in the contralateral eye (surgery, hyper-/mature cataract) may be associated with an aggressive response.

sections.title: Phacoanaphylactic Clinical & Management
content: Clinical Features: Recent trauma/surgery, exposed lens protein, AC flare + cells ± hypopyon, KPs, synechiae (PS + PAS), angle usually open (but ± PAS); IOP may be high, normal, or low.
Treatment of Inflammatory Process: Topical steroid (e.g. dexamethasone 0.1% hourly) and surgical removal of any retained lens fragments.
Treatment of iIOP: Medical—topical (e.g. β-blocker, α2-agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) or systemic (e.g. acetazolamide) agents, as required.
Contralateral Eye: Consider removal by intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCe) to reduce lens protein exposure.

sections.title: Lens Subluxation / Dislocation
content: Mechanism: Pupillary block by anterior lens subluxation or complete dislocation into the AC; possible coincident angle abnormality (e.g. Marfan’s syndrome).
Clinical: iIOP, subluxed/dislocated lens ± corneal oedema (if acute or lenticulocorneal touch); lenticular astigmatism and variable refraction.
Positional Management: Dilate and lie patient supine (encourage posterior movement), then constrict (keep lens behind pupil).
Surgical: Early lens extraction if positional measures fail, complete dislocation to AC, cataract, or recurrence. Often requires vitreoretinal approach.

sections.title: Steroid-Induced: Mechanisms & Rx
sections.content: Exogenous/endogenous steroids decrease outflow facility. POAG patients are particularly sensitive. Mechanisms include prostaglandin inhibition (e.g. PGF2A) and structural changes in ECM (glycosaminoglycans) and trabecular meshwork (cross-linking of actins). Always check for steroid use (anabolics, skin/hemorrhoid creams, inhaled, oral courses for asthma/COPD). Treatment: Decrease frequency/potency or stop steroid (± steroid-sparing agent); if essential, treat as POAG. SLT may be helpful.

rows: Red Cell
Hyphaema (traumatic) blocks TM. Rebleed 10% risk at ~5d. Sickle-cell patients harder to treat (acidosis from CAIs worsens sickling).
Strict bed rest, topical steroid, mydriatic/cycloplegic, topical/systemic IOP agents. Surgical: AC paracentesis ± washout. Refractory: Trabeculectomy.
Ghost Cell
Vitreous hemorrhage leads to TM blockage by degenerate RBCs (tan-colored) usually 2–4wk post-hemorrhage.
Medical treatment (as for POAG) usually sufficient. If failure: AC washout + vitrectomy.

sections.title: Other Open-Angle Varieties
content: Angle Recession: Blunt trauma risk; 10% glaucoma risk at 10y. Look for asymmetry of AC depth, pupil, and angle. Screen 3mo, 6mo, yearly. Treat as POAG.

Raised Episcleral Venous Pressure: From vascular abnormalities (Sturge–Weber, orbital varices, AV fistulae, SVC obstruction). Signs: Engorged veins, chemosis, proptosis, blood in Schlemm's canal. Surgery is hazardous (refractory uveal effusion).

Tumours: iIOP via TM clogging/infiltration, rubeosis, or 2° angle closure. 20% of malignant melanoma associated with iIOP. Suspect in atypical unilateral glaucoma. B-scan essential if posterior view poor.
Schwartz–Matsuo Syndrome: Mild AC inflammation + iIOP from RRD. Photoreceptor outer segments obstruct TM. Resolves rapidly with retinal detachment surgical repair.

sections.title: Iridocorneal Endothelial (ICE) Syndrome
content: General: Unilateral condition; abnormal endothelium migrates across angle/TM/iris. Rare, typically 20–40y old females. 50% glaucoma risk. HSV possible cause.
Variants: Chandler syndrome (corneal focus), Essential iris atrophy (iris focus), Iris naevus (Cogan–Reese) syndrome (pigmented nodules).
Clinical: Unilateral pain, blurred vision, fine corneal guttata ('beaten metal'), corneal oedema, corectopia, pseudopolycoria.
Gonioscopy: Broad-based PAS inserting anterior to Schwalbe’s line.
Management: Specular microscopy for diagnosis. Treatment: Medical (β-blocker, α2-agonist, CAI, PGA), Surgery (trabeculectomy ± augmented/tube), or cyclodestruction.

rows: Iridoschisis
Bilateral splitting/atrophy of anterior iris leaf. Elderly. Associated with nanophthalmos.
Angle-closure: Nd-YAG PI. Open-angle: As for POAG.
PPD
Bilateral, dominantly inherited, childhood detection. Iridocorneal adhesions. 15% glaucoma risk.
Treat glaucoma as for POAG.
Epithelial Downgrowth
Trauma/surgery allows epithelium to proliferate on endothelium/angle. Poor prognosis.
Difficult. Lower IOP (POAG style), intracameral 5-FU, extensive surgical excision.
Fuchs’ Endothelial Dystrophy
Peripheral corneal oedema causes 2° angle closure, especially in at-risk eyes with shallow AC.
Refer to primary corneal dystrophy management.

content.explanation: Mechanism: Posterior misdirection of aqueous into vitreous causing anterior displacement of vitreous, ciliary processes, and lens/PCIOL.

sections.title: Aqueous Misdirection Management
content: Risk Factors: Short axial length, chronic angle closure, previous acute closure, nanophthalmos, uveal effusion, surgery (trab, tube, cataract), laser PI, miotics.
Diagnosis: Acute iIOP, shallow/flat AC, patent PI present (no pupillary block/bombé), no choroidal detachment/hemorrhage.

Initial Medical: Patent PI check (repeat if needed), Dilate (Atropine 1% 3x/d + Phenylephrine 2.5% 4x/d), Systemic (Acetazolamide IV stat then PO + mannitol/glycerol), Topical (β-blocker + Apraclonidine).
Laser Intervention: YAG anterior vitreous disruption (capsulotomy/hyaloidotomy); Argon laser to ciliary processes; Trans-scleral cyclodiode photocoagulation.
Surgery (Goal: Uni-chamber eye): Peripheral zonulo-hyaloidectomy is key.
Phakic Surgery: VPV procedure (vitrectomy–phacoemulsification–vitrectomy) or phaco/ECCE + capsulotomy + vitrectomy.
Aphakic/Pseudophakic Surgery: Pars plana vitrectomy and posterior capsulotomy.

sections.title: Post-Cataract & VR Surgery
content: Post-Cataract Spike: Retained viscoelastic, lens fragments, or inflammation. Prophylaxis: Acetazolamide SR 250mg stat.
Post-Cataract Rare Causes: Suprachoroidal hemorrhage, phacolysis, phacoanaphylaxis, Amsler hemorrhage (Fuchs’ heterochromic), epithelial downgrowth, aqueous misdirection, UGH syndrome.
Intraocular Gas (SF6, C3F8): iIOP from expansion/overfill. Rx: Short-term medical (Acetazolamide SR 250mg 2x/d for 5d) or gas removal.
Scleral Buckles: 2° angle closure from ciliary body swelling/choroidal detachment. Usually resolves; medical treatment interim.
Silicone Oil: Oil in AC blocks TM. Rx: Medical; cyclodestruction if persistent. Early removal (<6mo) helps; late removal (>6mo) less effective due to macrophage incorporation.
Vitrectomy: Increases risk of rubeosis in PDR and ghost cell glaucoma.
